status_reason: Material, quantity (API concentration) and location (feed frame) are known, but the old calibration cannot be approved for the new blend because NIR chemometric models are built and validated for a specific matrix, and adding Raman means a new fused model that needs its own calibration and validation.
answer: Do not reuse the old NIR calibration: NIR quantitation relies on chemometric models built and validated for a specific matrix, so the new API/excipient blend needs a re-test and most likely a new calibration. Adding Raman does not rescue the old model; Raman adds complementary backbone information to NIR, and a fused NIR+Raman PLS model is a new model that has been reported to predict API potency in the feed frame more accurately than single-method models in one study, so it is worth testing against a recalibrated NIR model on the same validation data. The first experiment should test the old model on the new blend, build a new NIR model and a fused NIR+Raman model in the feed frame, and compare both against independent laboratory reference analyses.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflection with a new calibration for the new blend in the feed frame, compared against fused NIR + Raman
inline.probe: NIR diffuse reflection probe (existing pilot probe type, to be confirmed)
inline.install: in the feed frame of the rotary tablet press, as in the existing pilot
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica fiber (350–2400 nm), which covers most of the NIR range 780–2500 nm
inline.test_against: NIR + Raman (785 nm excitation) with low-level fusion of synchronised spectra and PLS
inline.not_final_because: The old calibration is untested on the new matrix, the new API/excipient identities and concentration range are unknown, a new model needs independent laboratory reference values, and any fusion gain is a hypothesis to be proven on this formulation.

problems.text: The existing calibration cannot be assumed valid for the new formulation: NIR calibrations are chemometric models built and validated for a specific matrix, so a different API and excipient blend is a new matrix and the old model must be re-tested and most likely replaced by a new calibration.

Adding Raman does not keep the old calibration valid: Raman adds complementary information and a combined NIR+Raman model is built on newly fused data, which is a new model needing its own calibration and validation, and whether fusion helps this formulation is a hypothesis.
Raman signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence of many organic compounds, so check whether the new API or excipients fluoresce at 785 nm before relying on Raman.
For a fused model the NIR and Raman spectra must be time-synchronised because the methods have different acquisition rates, and in a heterogeneous powder both should ideally see the same spot.

methods.why: NIR diffuse reflection suits powders, is the most common online fiber-probe method and is already installed in the feed frame, but needs a new chemometric model for the new matrix.

NIR sees hydrogen bonds and polar groups while Raman sees the molecular backbone and non-polar groups, and a feed-frame study reported fused PLS models predicted API potency more accurately than single-method models.
A Raman contact probe with 785 nm excitation is used in the feed frame for blend potency and has high selectivity for powders, but it is weak and can be masked by fluorescence.
Strong mid-IR absorption limits MIR to very thin layers and ATR suits liquids, pastes and soft solids, not a flowing powder in a feed frame.

questions.q: What are the new API and excipients, and what API concentration range must be covered?
questions.why: The model must be built for the new matrix and its concentration range.

questions.q: Which independent laboratory reference method and how many reference samples can you provide for the new blend?
questions.why: A new calibration and its validation require reference values from independent analyses.

questions.q: Which NIR probe, spectrometer range and fiber does the current pilot use, and how was the old calibration built and validated?
questions.why: This determines whether the existing hardware can be reused and how to re-test the old model.

questions.q: Do the new API or excipients show fluorescence, or have you seen Raman spectra of them?
questions.why: Fluorescence can mask Raman signals and decide whether Raman is usable.

questions.q: What accuracy and measurement rate does the process need to accept a model?
questions.why: Go/no-go criteria for single and fused models must come from you.

experiment.objective: Determine whether a new NIR calibration or a fused NIR+Raman model best predicts API concentration of the new blend in the feed frame.
steps: Apply the old NIR calibration to spectra of the new blend and compare predictions with independent laboratory reference values to document whether it fails.
Prepare new-blend samples across the target API range and record NIR diffuse reflection and 785 nm Raman spectra in the feed frame, time-synchronised.
Check the Raman spectra for fluorescence background and identify key spectral features of the new API in both methods.
Build a new NIR PLS model, a Raman PLS model and a low-level fused NIR+Raman PLS model on the same calibration set.
Compare all models on the same independent validation set against the laboratory reference values and the client's criteria.
references: Independent laboratory assay of API concentration (method to be named by the client) on samples taken at the feed frame

pathway.key_features: No spectra supplied yet; identify the new API bands in NIR (hydrogen bonds, polar groups) and Raman (molecular backbone, non-polar groups) during the trial.
pathway.path_reason: A chemometric model can only be chosen after multi-method trials on the new blend have identified key spectral features.

multispectral.why: NIR detects hydrogen bonds and asymmetric polar groups while Raman provides the molecular backbone and symmetrical non-polar groups, and NIR+Raman fusion was reported to improve API potency prediction in the feed frame.
multispectral.test: Build the fused PLS model and the best single-method model on the same calibration data and accept fusion only if it beats the single model on the same independent validation set; a combined NIRaman probe that fits the feed frame avoids spot mismatch, otherwise separate probes must at least be time-synchronised.

assumptions: The existing pilot uses an NIR diffuse reflection probe in the feed frame.
The new blend is a powder fed through the same tablet press feed frame.
